# Batch record 50 raw clips in one session

A busy owner may not have time to film each day. This guide helps you plan one session for 50 short answers. Start with a list of real questions, then keep track of each clip as you go.

**The path:** 50 real questions → Film in groups → Check 50 files → Editor.

**Use this when:** The team has agreed to make a 50-clip batch and has enough real questions to fill it.

## Inputs
- A numbered list of 50 distinct questions, each with a real source and a topic. Use [the topic-planning task](https://local-service-spotlight.github.io/task-library/?task=map-out-one-minute-video-topics-using-topic-wheel#task-map-out-one-minute-video-topics-using-topic-wheel) first if the list is missing.
- A willing speaker who knows the answers; a charged phone, stand, free storage, and a quiet place.
- A planned 2–3 hour block from the source method. Treat this as a planning estimate, not a promise that 50 good answers will fit.
- An approved raw folder, tracker, upload access, and named editor. Note permission and private-content limits before filming.

## First-run prompt

> Help me prepare and reconcile a 50-question filming batch. Use only the real questions and sources I provide. Group and number them, flag duplicates, then match saved takes to questions. Show usable distinct answers out of 50 and list any missing items. Do not treat an extra take as a new answer.

## Steps
1. Number the questions 01–50. Group related ones. Remove duplicates and questions the speaker cannot answer. Fill the gaps from real sources before calling the list ready.
2. Build the tracker before filming: question number, exact question, source, topic, take name, file link, length, review state, next owner. A question number spoken aloud helps, but does not replace this log.
3. Test the camera, storage, light, and microphone. Keep one setup while it works; fix it if light, noise, battery, or framing changes. Use silent checks for agents and record any sound-review gap.
4. Film one answer per file. Say the question number, then follow [one-minute video guide](https://blitzmetrics.com/one-minute-video-guide/): question, answer, and one true example. Aim for 45–90 seconds. Keep simple notes nearby.
5. Work in groups of 10–15, then take a short break. Check that those files saved and that the speaker still has clear answers. A rough word is fine; an incorrect answer or failed recording needs another take.
6. Track each take as you go. Mark a replacement take clearly and keep the original until the editor has the safe copy. Do not invent filler questions or accept bad clips just to reach 50.
7. Upload to a batch folder named YYYY-MM-DD-batch-NN-topic within the existing raw folder. Keep one final candidate per question and link any alternate take. Confirm uploads finished.
8. Reconcile the question list against the tracker and saved files. Count distinct answered questions, not file count. Fifty files with three repeated questions is only 47 distinct answers.
9. Hand the checked batch and the exception list to [Upload the source to Drive and Descript](https://local-service-spotlight.github.io/task-library/?task=step-1-upload-video-to-google-drive-and-descript#task-step-1-upload-video-to-google-drive-and-descript). If only 47 pass, record 47 of 50 and the three missing items. The run is partial; make a new filming plan rather than claim completion.

## Definition of done (QA checklist)

- [ ] 50 distinct sourced questions have 50 usable mapped takes; duplicates and abandoned takes are excluded from the count.
- [ ] Each selected take has a clear answer, usable picture and sound, and permission notes.
- [ ] Every selected take is uploaded, linked in the tracker, and accessible to the editor.
- [ ] Any shortfall is counted and named. One session and the planned batch size describe the goal, not permission to hide failed work.

## Example(s)

**Fictional teaching example — not a real batch.** Maple Cycle plans 50 answers: 20 about booking a visit, 15 about shop services, and 15 about buying a used bike. Each question has a sample source note.

The teaching checklist starts with:

| Question | Topic | Selected take | Check |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 01: Do I need a booking? | Visits | `q01-take1.mp4` | 58 seconds; clear answer |
| 02: Can I send a photo first? | Visits | `q02-take2.mp4` | 65 seconds; replaces an interrupted take |
| 03: When will I get a quote? | Quotes | No usable take | The answer gave an unsupported promise |

In this sample, 47 of 50 distinct questions pass. The useful result is a 47-item handoff plus three named gaps. It is not “50 done,” even if the folder holds 54 files. A real run needs the full 50-row list, real file links, and review evidence.

## Handoff and Content Factory context

The editor gets the batch folder, 50-row question list, selected takes, rights notes, and exact pass/shortfall count. [Upload the source to Drive and Descript](https://local-service-spotlight.github.io/task-library/?task=step-1-upload-video-to-google-drive-and-descript#task-step-1-upload-video-to-google-drive-and-descript) starts processing the accepted footage; the speaker owns any agreed missing takes.

This task serves **Produce** in the [Content Factory](https://blitzmetrics.com/content-factory/). Produce makes or prepares source material. Process edits it, Post puts approved work on a channel, and Promote helps it reach people. Only the steps and handoff above are part of this task.

## When this runs

This is one planned session. Repeat only when the content plan calls for another batch. No fixed repeat rate is established by this task.

## Run with an agent

The agent can prepare the plan, organize allowed files, and check the evidence it can actually access. A person records real stories, supplies permission, or resolves an account step when needed. Save the current state in the project files and tracker. A model name does not create memory, access, a scheduler, or permission to act.

For all agent media checks, keep the player muted and its volume at zero before playback. If that cannot be checked, use captions, metadata, or still frames. Do not claim sound quality was heard when it was not.

## Write up the real run

For every actual attempt, [write the run’s meta article](https://blitzmetrics.com/meta-article-prompt/). Link this exact task and its source revision. State the start, work done, evidence, result, gaps, and next owner. Keep failed, partial, and blocked work visible. Writing the record does not authorize publishing it.

Use one stable execution ID for this task’s actual run. Internal retries, checks, and new versions do not add runs. A separately scoped child task may have its own ID linked to the parent. A teaching example has no real execution ID and must not enter the run count. Follow the [recipe and meta-article guide](https://localservicespotlight.com/meta-articles/) for that distinction.

- **Phase:** Produce
- **Importance:** 4/5 `●●●●○` — frequency 4, revenue 3, gating 3 (runs every factory cycle or weekly)
- **Suggested previous station:** `map-out-one-minute-video-topics-using-topic-wheel`

These stations are generated neighbors, not verified prerequisites or handoffs. Follow the task’s actual Inputs and Handoff sections.
- **Handoff:** Raw files in Content Library `01-Raw/` plus a tracker row (question, date, speaker). Next skill never needs the chat — it needs the files.

## Model routing (same factory, any engine)

- **This task's lane:** `any` — Any capable chat model (Claude, ChatGPT, Grok, Gemini). SOP following, drafts, checklists.
- **Single-engine path:** Use the capable AI app you already have. Check its required tools and access before starting. Pass the actual result and proof to the next task.
- **Optional multi-engine:** A tested local model may draft; a stronger model may review facts and voice. Use supported tools for approved actions. Pick models from observed quality and cost; a model name does not prove it can run this task.
- **Never** store the working state in one vendor's memory. Files in the Content Library are the bridge.

The contributor status in the source header is preserved. It is not a claim that this draft has been independently accepted or that a real run has passed. The worked example above is for teaching only.

# Capture client stories on phone

A happy client can explain your work in their own words. This guide helps you save that story with their name and clear permission. First, ask what changed and where they are happy for the story to appear.

**The path:** Permission → Client’s own story → Facts and files → Review.

**Use this when:** A real client has a specific result and agrees to tell the story on camera.

## Inputs
- A real client, a specific project or change, and evidence for any stated numbers.
- Permission to record and a separate clear record of allowed use of the person’s name, face, words, and company or location. Capture limits and the date.
- A phone, a quiet location, and permission to film the location and supporting shots.
- The approved raw folder, upload access, tracker, and named reviewer who will check facts and permission.

## First-run prompt

> Help me capture a client story from the facts and permission I provide. Draft plain interview questions, an attribution line, and a shot list. Flag claims that lack proof and uses that are not agreed. After capture, check the file package and prepare a factual handoff for review.

## Steps
1. Ask what may be recorded and where it may be used. Explain the intended article or channel. Record the answer in the project’s permission log; do not infer public use from a person agreeing to a private call.
2. Check the person’s full name and the right role, company, or city for the story. For a homeowner, do not invent a job title or company. Let the person confirm the attribution line.
3. Frame the person at eye level in a real setting. Check light, framing, and microphone. Keep private papers, addresses, or other people out of the shot unless cleared.
4. Ask four plain questions: What was the problem? What work was done? What changed? Who would this help? Let the client answer in their own words. Follow up on vague praise with “What is one example?”
5. When the client gives a number, note its source and what period it covers. If it cannot be checked, keep it as a claim for review or omit it from the finished piece. Do not turn a guess into a proven result.
6. Ask the client to confirm their name and attribution on camera when practical. Capture a still photo and about 30–60 seconds of supporting footage, called b-roll, such as the finished work. If consent or the setting prevents a shot, record that gap.
7. Name the video, photo, and supporting footage YYYY-MM-DD-clientname-story with a type or take suffix. Upload to the approved folder and log the links, permission, attribution, result evidence, and reviewer.
8. Send the raw package for review through [Upload the source to Drive and Descript](https://local-service-spotlight.github.io/task-library/?task=step-1-upload-video-to-google-drive-and-descript#task-step-1-upload-video-to-google-drive-and-descript). A missing name, usage permission, or unverified claim stays clearly flagged before any public use.

## Definition of done (QA checklist)

- [ ] The story describes a specific real change in the client’s own words.
- [ ] Full attribution fits the person and is confirmed; permission covers the proposed use.
- [ ] Claims have evidence or are marked unverified. A named quote alone does not prove a number.
- [ ] Video, a still image, and supporting footage are saved, or the exact capture gap is recorded.
- [ ] The reviewer can open the files and see all privacy or publication limits.

## Example(s)

**Fictional teaching example — invented people and shop, not a testimonial to publish.** Morgan, a made-up customer of Maple Cycle, says: “I did not know if the bike was worth fixing. They gave me a written quote before doing the work, so I could choose.”

The teaching attribution is “Morgan Lane, local customer.” The sample story makes no sales or safety claim. Its evidence would be the approved quote and the customer’s confirmation. A shot of the quote would hide contact details and the home address.

The teaching permission note says “website story and shop social posts; no paid ads agreed.” That means an editor could prepare those drafts after a real consent check, but an ad would need its own authority and usage check. Do not copy this invented quote into a real client page.

## Handoff and Content Factory context

The editor receives the files and permission limits. The reviewer uses [Verify testimonials with full attribution](https://local-service-spotlight.github.io/task-library/?task=verify-testimonials-with-full-attribution#task-verify-testimonials-with-full-attribution) before public use. [Upload the source to Drive and Descript](https://local-service-spotlight.github.io/task-library/?task=step-1-upload-video-to-google-drive-and-descript#task-step-1-upload-video-to-google-drive-and-descript) is the source-file handoff; a story is not automatically cleared for ads.

This task serves **Produce** in the [Content Factory](https://blitzmetrics.com/content-factory/). Produce makes or prepares source material. Process edits it, Post puts approved work on a channel, and Promote helps it reach people. Only the steps and handoff above are part of this task.

Run for each willing client story when a real result exists. This task sets no automatic outreach or recurring filming schedule.

## Run with an agent

The agent can prepare the plan, organize allowed files, and check the evidence it can actually access. A person records real stories, supplies permission, or resolves an account step when needed. For all agent media checks, keep the player muted and its volume at zero before playback. If that cannot be checked, use captions, metadata, or still frames. Do not claim sound quality was heard when it was not.

---
name: create-a-3-minute-why-video
description: "Tell the true story behind your work in a short video. Help a new viewer see who you serve and why."
category: Content Factory — Produce
stage: Produce
definitive_article: /social-amplification
status: complete
---

# Create a 3-minute WHY video

People may know what you sell but not why you care. This guide helps an owner tell the true story behind the work. Start with one event that shaped your choice, then explain what it means for the people you serve.

**The path:** True origin story → Three speaking notes → Short video → Editor.

**Use this when:** The owner’s purpose and business goals are clear but there is no useful video that explains them.

## Inputs
- The owner’s stated purpose, current offer, and agreed business goals. Use the real source document, not an agent’s guessed memory.
- A true origin story the owner is willing to share and the facts needed to check it.
- The owner, a phone, and a real place connected to the story, with permission to film there.
- The approved raw folder, tracker access, and an editor. Record any people or details that must stay private.

## First-run prompt

> Help me shape my true origin story into three speaking notes for a three-minute video. Use my goals, offer, and facts. Flag anything you cannot verify. Give me a plain opening, a review checklist, and a file handoff; do not invent my biography or claim the video is ready for an ad.

## Steps
1. Read the agreed goals and offer with the owner. Write one plain sentence about who the business helps and why the owner does this work. If the purpose is not yet clear, draft that sentence for the owner to resolve before filming.
2. Choose one true moment that shows the purpose. Identify what happened, what the owner learned, and what changed in the work. Remove facts that cannot be confirmed; do not add drama to make the story stronger.
3. Make three speaking notes: the origin moment; who the owner serves and what they believe; what that means for a customer today. Practice saying the notes aloud without reading a script.
4. Set the phone in a real location linked to the story. Check the picture and microphone input. Keep private details out of the frame. The person, rather than a logo or stock scene, carries this story.
5. Record a take of about three minutes. Make the purpose clear in the first 30 seconds, then tell the example. This length is the source task’s format; it is not proof that the video fits a future ad placement.
6. Review the facts and meaning. Can a new viewer explain who this helps and why the owner cares? Keep a natural take; redo a failed recording or false claim. Use silent agent checks and name any remaining sound-review need.
7. Name the file YYYY-MM-DD-brandname-why-video with a take suffix if needed. Upload it, confirm the saved link, and log the source facts, purpose, length, rights, and next editor.
8. Queue it for [Upload the source to Drive and Descript](https://local-service-spotlight.github.io/task-library/?task=step-1-upload-video-to-google-drive-and-descript#task-step-1-upload-video-to-google-drive-and-descript). In the [Topic Wheel](https://blitzmetrics.com/topic-wheel/), this story belongs in WHY on the outside; the offer remains WHAT at the center. An About-page or ad version is a later editorial choice.

## Definition of done (QA checklist)

- [ ] The purpose is plain within the first 30 seconds, and a true origin moment supports it.
- [ ] The story names who the business serves and explains a useful customer meaning.
- [ ] The take is roughly three minutes; any format exception is stated and accepted.
- [ ] The raw file, facts, permissions, and review state are saved and handed to an editor.
- [ ] No later ad eligibility, performance, or public use is assumed from making the video.

## Example(s)

**Fictional teaching example — not a founder biography.** Alex, the made-up owner of Maple Cycle, uses these notes for a sample three-minute story:

| Part | Speaking note | What it teaches |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Opening | “I opened this shop so people can ask basic bike questions without feeling silly.” | Clear purpose |
| Origin | “When I first rode to work, I did not know how to ask for help at a repair shop.” | One specific moment, not a slogan |
| Customer meaning | “We explain the work and quote before you choose what to do.” | What the belief changes in the service |

The sample outline allows 30 seconds for the purpose, 90 for the story, and 60 for its meaning. Those are planning notes, not measured video times. A real recording must use the real owner’s story; never give Alex’s invented past to another person.

# Create a 3×3 video grid

A list of random video ideas can leave gaps. This guide helps an owner plan nine clips on three useful topics. Start with what you sell, then choose stories, lessons, and offer answers that help the right people.

**The path:** Three topics → Nine clear prompts → Nine saved takes → Editor.

- Three HOW topics from the [Topic Wheel](https://blitzmetrics.com/topic-wheel/) that support the actual offer, plus real questions, stories, and proof for those topics.
- The current [SEO Tree](https://blitzmetrics.com/seo-tree/) page map, so the editor knows which owned topic page each future piece should support.
- The speaker, phone, approved raw folder, tracker access, and a named editor. Allow enough filming time; a fixed half-day is a planning choice, not a promise.

## First-run prompt

> Build a three-topic by three-purpose video grid from my actual offer, stories, questions, and page map. Label story, teaching, and offer cells. Keep source links with each prompt and flag any invented or missing proof. After filming, count distinct usable cells and make the editor’s handoff.

## Steps
1. Select three related HOW topics where the business has real knowledge. Check how each supports the WHAT offer at the center of the Topic Wheel. Keep WHY stories on the outside.
2. Draw a table with three topic rows and three purpose columns: story/WHY, teaching/HOW, and offer or proof/WHAT. This is the purpose-based grid variant in this task source. The one-minute guide also describes concept/example/objection variations; label the chosen variant instead of mixing both systems mid-grid.
3. Write one prompt in every cell. Use a real story for the story cell, a useful question for teaching, and a true offer answer or supported result for the final cell. Link each prompt to its source. Do not fill a proof cell with a made-up win.
4. Give each cell a short ID such as A1. Add topic, purpose, question source, intended viewer, and the owned page that the later piece should support. Page-map neighbors are not automatic prerequisites.
5. Record one clear answer per cell using [one-minute video guide](https://blitzmetrics.com/one-minute-video-guide/). Aim for 45–90 seconds. Keep the person’s own words, and record a new take when facts, sound, or picture fail.
6. Save files as YYYY-MM-DD-topic-cellID-person. Use a take suffix for repeats. Upload into the existing raw folder and link the selected take for every cell in the tracker.
7. Review nine distinct purposes and nine usable takes. Count a repeated file once. If one cell has no real proof, mark the gap and agree on a truthful offer explanation or another supported prompt before filming it.

Hand the grid to [Upload the source to Drive and Descript](https://local-service-spotlight.github.io/task-library/?task=step-1-upload-video-to-google-drive-and-descript#task-step-1-upload-video-to-google-drive-and-descript). - [ ] All nine selected files open for the editor and match the tracker.
- [ ] Any missing cell is named; nine planned ideas are not nine completed videos.

# Film casual team conversations

Your team solves useful problems each day. A real talk can help others learn how you think. This guide shows you how to record the talk, mark private parts, and give the best moments to an editor.

**The path:** Agree on limits → Record real work → Mark useful moments → Editor.

**Use this when:** A real work discussion has a useful lesson and everyone involved agrees to the recording and planned use.

## Inputs
- A real planned team talk, such as a project review or a discussion of a problem.
- Agreement from everyone recorded and a list of facts, names, or screens that must stay private.
- A phone or the team’s approved recorder, enough storage, and a position that captures all speakers.
- The raw folder, tracker access, and the editor who will review highlights and private sections.

## First-run prompt

> Use our real discussion brief to make a short recording plan. After the talk, turn my time notes into an editor’s cut list. Keep proposals separate from measured results. List the exact private sections, permission gaps, and the next owner. Do not stage the conversation or publish it.

## Steps
1. Explain why the talk may become content. Confirm who agrees and what stays private. If someone does not agree, leave them out of the recording or keep the discussion unrecorded.
2. Set the camera where it can show the group and capture each voice. A wide shot may suit a table discussion. Run a short test; change the setup if a speaker is off-screen or the input is weak.
3. Record the real talk. Start with a short statement of the problem so the editor has context. Do not stage disagreement, invent a client issue, or repeat a conversation as if it were the first event.
4. Let each person finish their point. Keep the recording running through useful context, but pause when private material or a new person enters. Record the gap so later viewers are not misled by a cut.
5. While the discussion is fresh, note the strongest two or three moments with time ranges. For each, write the question, the useful idea, and any decision. A lively clip without enough context may need a longer cut.
6. Make a separate list of private sections with start/end times and what must be removed. Do not rely on “blur sensitive things” as the only instruction.
7. Save the original unchanged. Name it YYYY-MM-DD-topic-team-convo. Upload it to the approved raw folder, then add the link, speaker names, permission state, highlights, and edit limits to the tracker.
8. Hand off to [Upload the source to Drive and Descript](https://local-service-spotlight.github.io/task-library/?task=step-1-upload-video-to-google-drive-and-descript#task-step-1-upload-video-to-google-drive-and-descript). Use “Raw — needs private-content review” if redactions remain; the source file being uploaded does not make it safe to post.

## Definition of done (QA checklist)

- [ ] The recording captures real work with agreement from the recorded people.

- [ ] Two or three useful moments have time ranges and enough context for an editor.
- [ ] Private segments have specific edit instructions and a named reviewer.
- [ ] The original and tracker row are saved and accessible to the editor.

| 03:10–04:05 | A staff member suggests asking the customer to choose a pickup day | Candidate teaching clip; label it as a proposal |
| 06:02–06:30 | A sample customer’s contact details appear | Remove the whole section before public use |
| 09:00–10:10 | The team chooses a small test | Keep the decision; do not claim the test worked |

# Film conference presentations

A talk can hold lessons worth sharing after the event. This guide helps a speaker save the talk and the questions that follow. First, check what the event allows and who will run the camera.

**The path:** Event permission → Talk and allowed Q&A → Files and notes → Editor.

**Use this when:** You or a client has a confirmed speaking slot and permission to capture it.

## Inputs
- A confirmed event, speaker, session time, and the organizer’s recording and reuse terms.
- A camera operator or agreed fixed setup, charged phone, stand, storage, and a clear view.
- An audio plan. If a venue feed or official recording is available, ask how it may be received and used; do not assume it is included.
- The raw folder, tracker access, and named speaker/editor contacts. Get the session title and any allowed slide source.

## First-run prompt

> Use the confirmed event and rights I provide to prepare a recording checklist. Then turn the actual files and time notes into an intake index. Identify missing ranges, allowed questions, and the next editor. Keep speaking evidence precise; do not invent an endorsement or claim a full recording if a part is missing.

## Steps
1. Confirm recording and later use with the organizer before the event. Ask about official footage and audience questions. Use a personal backup only if it is allowed; an official recording does not grant extra recording rights.
2. Assign the operator and test the view and audio input before the room fills. Choose a stable position without blocking attendees. Check power and storage against the planned session length.
3. Capture the host’s introduction if permitted. Save the wording and context as proof of that introduction; it does not by itself prove every expertise or endorsement claim.
4. Record the talk from start to finish when allowed. If recording stops, write the missing time range. Do not label a partial recording as the full talk.
5. Record the permitted questions and answers. If an audience member is not cleared to appear, follow the event’s method for keeping them out or omit that segment. Transcribe only the questions you may use.
6. Capture approved stills and supporting shots of the speaker and event. Keep the source date and event name with each. Avoid badges, private screens, or attendees who are not cleared.
7. Save the originals as YYYY-MM-DD-eventname-talk with part numbers where needed. Upload video, separate audio if any, and photos. Note the intro range, talk range, Q&A range, rights, and any gaps.
8. Add useful audience questions to the [Topic Wheel](https://blitzmetrics.com/topic-wheel/) topic queue with their event source. They may support a HOW topic or a story; they are not automatically the WHAT offer.
9. Send the indexed package to [Upload the source to Drive and Descript](https://local-service-spotlight.github.io/task-library/?task=step-1-upload-video-to-google-drive-and-descript#task-step-1-upload-video-to-google-drive-and-descript). # Map out one-minute video topics using Topic Wheel

It is hard to film when you do not know what to say. This guide helps an owner turn real questions and stories into a short video list. Start with what you sell and who it helps, then choose useful topics.

**The path:** Clear offer → Useful topics → True stories and questions → Video queue.

**Use this when:** The recording queue is empty, off-topic, or hard to link to the business offer.

## Inputs
- The current offer, intended customer, and owner’s real purpose and goals.
- Real source material: customer questions, call notes, comments, FAQs, allowed event questions, and true owner or partner stories.
- The current [SEO Tree](https://blitzmetrics.com/seo-tree/) map of owned topic pages, or a record that the page map is still missing.
- A sheet or drawing tool and edit access to the content tracker. Name the person who can approve the plan and the person who will record.

## First-run prompt

> Use my current offer, true stories, customer questions, and page map to build a Topic Wheel and recording queue. Put WHAT at the center, HOW topics in the middle, and WHY stories outside. Keep sources and permission notes. Do not invent people, relationships, demand counts, or page links.

## Steps
1. Use the current [Topic Wheel](https://blitzmetrics.com/topic-wheel/) definitions: WHAT is the product or service at the center; HOW is the middle ring of topics and expertise; WHY is the outer ring of people and true stories. The audience moves from stories toward the offer, but planning starts with the offer.
2. Write one clear sentence for WHAT. State the actual product or service and who it is for. Do not replace the offer with a vague mission line.
3. List about three to seven HOW topics that support the offer and match real expertise. Merge duplicates. Keep the owner’s plain words instead of invented framework names.
4. For each topic, collect real WHY stories, people, and allowed collaborations. Record the source and permission state. A wish to work with someone is not an existing relationship.
5. Add real customer questions under the matching topics. Preserve the question wording and source in the private tracker. Questions can produce teaching clips; they are not themselves the WHAT ring.
6. Match topics to the owned page map. Use the topic hub for the main explanation and specific stories as supporting pages when appropriate. Mark a missing page as a gap instead of linking an unrelated page.
7. Create one recording-queue row per useful prompt: question or story, source, topic, link to the offer, intended viewer, page home, speaker, and state. Rank by observed repeat questions and the agreed business need. If frequency was not measured, say so.
8. Review the queue with the plan owner. Hand accepted prompts to [Record one-minute videos](https://local-service-spotlight.github.io/task-library/?task=record-one-minute-videos#task-record-one-minute-videos) or an agreed [50-clip batch](https://local-service-spotlight.github.io/task-library/?task=batch-record-50-raw-clips-in-one-session#task-batch-record-50-raw-clips-in-one-session). Save the wheel, source list, and current queue together.
9. The source calls for a monthly refresh. Keep answered items linked to their clips; do not erase history. Add new questions and mark replaced or stale prompts. A calendar job needs an agreed owner, timezone, access, and trigger before it can run.

## Definition of done (QA checklist)

- [ ] The wheel uses WHAT center, HOW middle, and WHY outside, with the actual offer stated.
- [ ] Each selected topic relates to the offer; each story or question has a traceable source.
- [ ] The queue has a clear prompt, topic, speaker, and owned-page destination or named page gap.
- [ ] Priority is based on evidence or labeled judgment, with no fabricated demand counts.
- [ ] Accepted prompts and prior answers remain findable for recording and later review.

## Example(s)

**Fictional teaching example — not a real business plan or customer research.** Maple Cycle’s sample wheel has WHAT at the center: “Bike repair quotes and service for local riders.” Its HOW topics are repair quotes, planning a shop visit, and used-bike questions. An outside WHY story is Alex’s wish to make basic questions feel welcome.

| Prompt | Ring or topic use | Sample source | Recording choice |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Why did Alex open the shop? | WHY story | Invented founder note | One origin story |
| Can I send a photo before a visit? | HOW: planning a visit | Invented customer email | One teaching answer |
| What does a quote visit include? | WHAT: current offer | Invented service sheet | One offer explanation |

The sample does not say “customers ask this 20 times a week,” because no real count exists. In a real queue, replace each invented source with the actual record and set the next speaker before filming.

The named speaker receives accepted prompts through [Record one-minute videos](https://local-service-spotlight.github.io/task-library/?task=record-one-minute-videos#task-record-one-minute-videos). Create the first wheel once. The source proposes a monthly refresh and updates when new questions arrive. Treat monthly as a planned review until a real owner and schedule have been configured; no reminder is installed by this guide.

## Run with an agent

The agent can prepare the plan, organize allowed files, and check the evidence it can actually access. A person records real stories, supplies permission, or resolves an account step when needed. Save the current state in the project files and tracker. A model name does not create memory, access, a scheduler, or permission to act.

# Record one-minute videos

You know things your customers need to know. This guide helps a business owner turn one real question into a short video. Pick a question, give a clear answer, and save the file for your team.

**The path:** Real question → One short answer → Saved clip → Editor.

**Use this when:** You have a real customer question and need a new source clip.

## Inputs
- One question from a call, email, comment, or the topic queue. Keep a link or private note that shows where it came from.
- The owner or team member who knows the answer, a charged phone, and a quiet place with good light.
- Permission from anyone who will be shown. Keep private customer details out of the shot.
- The brand’s approved raw-video folder and content tracker, plus access to add files and rows. Name the person who will edit the clip.

## First-run prompt

> Use the question and source I give you to help me plan one short video. Give me three speaking notes, a file name, and a tracker row. Ask only for facts you need. Do not write a fake customer story. Check the saved clip and list what is still unverified before handoff.

## Steps
1. Choose one question you can answer from real work. Note who needs the answer and what they should understand by the end. Use [Topic Wheel](https://blitzmetrics.com/topic-wheel/) to place it under the right topic; a question is not the WHAT ring. WHAT means the offer at the center.
2. Place the phone at eye level. Keep the lens clear, your face lit, and the background simple. Choose framing that fits the planned use. A vertical phone shot is a useful starting point for a short answer.
3. Make a short test. Check framing, the microphone input, and the saved file. For an agent review, use silent frames and available captions; mark sound quality unverified until someone has checked it under the allowed media rules.
4. Use three notes, not a script: the question, one true example, and why the answer helps. Say the question, answer it in plain words, then give the example. Do not make up a customer story or a result.
5. Aim for about one minute. The source guide accepts 45–90 seconds. Keep a useful take even if a word is rough. Record a new take if the answer is wrong, the sound fails, or the key point is missing; do not pass a broken take to save time.
6. Name the file YYYY-MM-DD-topic-person. If there is more than one take, add a take number so you do not overwrite the first. Upload it to the approved raw folder and wait for the upload to finish.
7. Open the saved file from its folder link without starting sound. Match its name and length to your local file. Add the source question, topic, length, permissions, file link, and editor to the tracker.
8. Mark it “Raw — ready for Process” only when the checks below pass. If a check is missing, state what is missing and who can resolve it. Hand off to [Upload the source to Drive and Descript](https://local-service-spotlight.github.io/task-library/?task=step-1-upload-video-to-google-drive-and-descript#task-step-1-upload-video-to-google-drive-and-descript).

- [ ] One real question and its source are recorded; the answer stays on that question.

- [ ] The saved link opens for the editor, and the tracker includes the topic, permission state, and next owner.

**Fictional teaching example — not a client result or completed run.** Maple Cycle is a made-up bike shop. Its owner, Alex, wants to answer this sample customer email: “Should I bring my bike in before asking for a repair quote?”

The teaching tracker row reads: topic = repair quotes; source = sample email; file = `2026-09-06-repair-quote-alex-take1.mp4`; length = 62 seconds; next role = editor. # Record screen shares of real audits

A screen full of charts can be hard to understand. This guide helps an owner or reviewer explain a real check in plain words. Start with the goal, then show what you found and what should happen next.

**The path:** Approved audit → Clear screen and narration → Findings and edit notes → Editor.

**Use this when:** An approved real audit is about to happen and it may be recorded for teaching or review.

## Inputs
- The actual audit task and checklist, the property to review, and authorization for that read or work. This recording guide does not grant permission to test or change systems.
- Permission to record and the agreed later uses. List private names, emails, account data, and other details to keep out.
- An approved screen recorder with microphone and screen-capture access; enough local storage. For the Zoom method below, use the desktop app and a host role or host-granted recording privilege.
- The approved raw folder, tracker, reviewer, and editor. Keep credentials out of the recording and all public evidence.

## First-run prompt

> Use the approved audit scope and checklist I provide to plan a clear screen recording. Give me a short goal statement, section prompts, and a privacy check. After capture, organize actual findings and time ranges. Do not run changes, assume a passed check, or expose private account details.

## Steps
1. Name the goal, what this recording will show, and who needs it. These are [Goals, Content, and Targeting](https://blitzmetrics.com/gct-business-strategy/). Link the exact audit checklist instead of improvising a new audit from this filming guide.
2. Close private tabs, notifications, password tools, and unrelated windows. Share only the needed window when possible. Choose examples and views the client has allowed. Keep a private list of any remaining redaction risks.
3. For an approved Zoom recording, start the meeting as host or get host permission to record. Select the intended screen or window and check that the needed text is readable. Check microphone input without playing sound through speakers.
4. Use Record, then Record on this Computer if offered. Confirm the recording indicator before beginning. If the approved recorder is Descript instead, use its current recording controls and verify the same screen, microphone, and file checks; do not assume Zoom’s controls apply.
5. For each real checklist item, say what you are checking, why it matters, what the screen shows, and the next action. Keep observations separate from guesses. An inaccessible view is “not checked,” not a pass.
6. Pause between sections and when private content may appear. Note time ranges for useful findings and sections that must be removed. A recording is not permission to click a live change or run an intrusive test.
7. For Zoom, stop recording, then end the meeting to begin local conversion. Wait for conversion to finish before moving or renaming the file; keep it on a local drive during conversion. For Descript or another approved recorder, verify its processing has finished before copying the saved file to the approved raw folder.
8. Name it YYYY-MM-DD-clientname-audit-topic. Save checklist results, evidence references, time ranges, and privacy notes with the tracker row. Review a redacted copy before public use; keep the original in its approved restricted location.
9. Hand the source and findings to [Upload the source to Drive and Descript](https://local-service-spotlight.github.io/task-library/?task=step-1-upload-video-to-google-drive-and-descript#task-step-1-upload-video-to-google-drive-and-descript). The actual audit’s own acceptance checks determine whether the audit passed. This task checks the recording package.

- [ ] The audit property, checklist, scope, and permitted recording use are stated.

- [ ] Missing checks are visible; the narration does not claim a result from a screen it could not inspect.
- [ ] The file has finished processing, is saved, and has time-based privacy and highlight notes.
- [ ] The named editor can access the allowed package; public-use clearance and sound review are explicit.

**Fictional teaching example — not an audit of a real site.** In a sample page review for Maple Cycle, a reviewer checks whether the “Book a visit” link reaches the intended booking page.

The narration is: “The goal is to help a rider book a visit. At 02:10, this button opens an old page. I checked the new page separately and it loads. The site editor should update the button and test it again.”

The sample result is one failed link check and one proposed fix. It is not “the site passed” or “bookings increased.” The cut list marks 04:15–04:25 for removal because a private email appears. A real handoff needs the actual page references, recording, permission, and retest evidence.

# Set up Content Library

Good files are hard to use when they sit in phones and chat threads. This guide helps a business owner put them in one clear home. Start with an approved folder, then make a log that shows each file and its next step.

**The path:** Approved home → Four clear stages → File log → Tested handoff.

**Use this when:** The brand needs its first content library or an agreed set of existing files needs to be organized.

## Inputs
- A brand-controlled Google Drive location and a person authorized to set its folders and sharing. Check whether it is My Drive or a Workspace shared drive.
- A bounded list of assets to organize, with their present locations, owners, permissions, and known duplicates. “All files” needs a stated scope.
- The current [Topic Wheel](https://blitzmetrics.com/topic-wheel/) topics, the raw-file intake location, and any existing library layout that must be preserved.
- Edit access for the folder and tracker, plus the names of the intake owner, editor, and person who controls access. Do not grant everyone full edit rights by default.

## First-run prompt

> Help me build or clean up the agreed content library from the locations and file list I provide. Preserve the existing approved structure and source trail. Draft the README and tracker, check ownership and access, and reconcile only the stated scope. Report exact gaps; do not delete originals, grant extra access, or schedule a job without authority.

## Steps
1. Confirm the library home with the brand owner. Use the existing approved structure if there is one. Record the location, access owner, scope of files, and limits before moving anything.
2. Check ownership, not just the name of the parent folder. In My Drive, a brand-owned folder does not make each uploaded file brand-owned. Where the brand has an approved Workspace shared drive, files belong to the organization. If using My Drive, record file owners and resolve the actual ownership plan with the access owner.
3. Create or map four stage folders: 01-Raw, 02-In-Process, 03-Published, and 04-Promote-Creatives. These reflect the [Content Factory](https://blitzmetrics.com/content-factory/) stages: make source material, edit it, publish it, and then distribute it. Do not mark content published just because it is placed in 03-Published.
4. Write a short root README. State who owns the library, where new files arrive, how to name them, where the tracker lives, and who takes the next step. Use YYYY-MM-DD-topic-person plus type or take suffix when needed. Keep original names in the tracker to preserve the source trail. Preserve each file extension unless you separately convert the file and verify the result.
5. Create a tracker with one row per source asset: asset ID, original name, current name, date, source link, topic, [GCT](https://blitzmetrics.com/gct-business-strategy/) notes, owner/permission state, stage, next person, and links to derived work. GCT means the goal, what this file shows, and who it is for.
6. Inventory the agreed assets before moving them. Copy or move only within the approved scope; do not delete originals or merge duplicate-looking files without checking them. Rename the working copy, file it in the right stage, and log each item. Keep unmatched or inaccessible files on an exception list.
7. Open the raw folder in Drive and use New → File upload or Folder upload, or drag the allowed files into it. Wait for completion. If a filename already exists, inspect the choice before overwriting a version; preserve distinct takes.
8. Check sharing with the access owner. Give the team only the roles needed for intake, editing, or review. Parent folder sharing can affect its contents. Use an approved restricted location for files that need tighter limits.
9. Test the handoff with one actual source file. Confirm the editor can open it and find its tracker row. Point [Upload the source to Drive and Descript](https://local-service-spotlight.github.io/task-library/?task=step-1-upload-video-to-google-drive-and-descript#task-step-1-upload-video-to-google-drive-and-descript) at the agreed intake. An existing worker may require a specific source path; record that path rather than assume it reads these folder names.
10. Reconcile files and rows within the agreed scope. Count found, logged, inaccessible, and unresolved assets. Save the README and exception list. The source proposes a weekly backlog review; configure that separately only when an owner, time, and access are agreed.

## Definition of done (QA checklist)

- [ ] The library location and actual file ownership model are recorded.
- [ ] The four stage folders are created or mapped to the existing layout, with a clear raw intake.
- [ ] The README and tracker explain naming, topic, stage, rights, and handoff.
- [ ] Every asset in the stated scope has a tracker row or a named exception; source copies and original names remain traceable.
- [ ] An actual recipient has checked access to a test file; missing access is not reported as ready.
- [ ] The backlog review is described without falsely claiming a scheduled job exists.

## Example(s)

**Fictional teaching example — no Drive folders or client files were created.** Maple Cycle’s sample scope is 12 phone clips and 4 photos. The teaching folder plan is:

```text
Maple Cycle Content
  README
  Content tracker
  01-Raw
  02-In-Process
  03-Published
  04-Promote-Creatives
```

One sample row maps original `IMG_0421.mov` to `2026-09-06-repair-quote-alex.mov`, topic “repair quotes,” stage “Raw,” next role “editor.” Its output links stay blank until real outputs exist.

If the sample intake finds 15 of the 16 planned assets and one phone is unavailable, the result is “15 logged; one photo still needed.” If the parent folder is brand-owned but this clip belongs to another person in My Drive, ownership is still unresolved. A neat folder tree is not proof that the brand controls every file.

## Handoff and Content Factory context

The intake owner receives the README, file log, and exceptions. The editor tests one source file and starts [Upload the source to Drive and Descript](https://local-service-spotlight.github.io/task-library/?task=step-1-upload-video-to-google-drive-and-descript#task-step-1-upload-video-to-google-drive-and-descript). The existing worker or upload task must use the verified intake path; this guide does not install or activate it.

This task serves **Produce** in the [Content Factory](https://blitzmetrics.com/content-factory/). Produce makes or prepares source material. Process edits it, Post puts approved work on a channel, and Promote helps it reach people. Only the steps and handoff above are part of this task.

## When this runs

The initial setup is a one-time task for the agreed scope. Normal intake happens as new assets arrive. A weekly raw-backlog review is the source recommendation, with items older than a week flagged for review; it becomes a real schedule only after configuration and a checked first run.

## Run with an agent

The agent can prepare the plan, organize allowed files, and check the evidence it can actually access. A person records real stories, supplies permission, or resolves an account step when needed. Save the current state in the project files and tracker. A model name does not create memory, access, a scheduler, or permission to act.

For all agent media checks, keep the player muted and its volume at zero before playback. If that cannot be checked, use captions, metadata, or still frames. Do not claim sound quality was heard when it was not.

## Write up the real run

For every actual attempt, [write the run’s meta article](https://blitzmetrics.com/meta-article-prompt/). Link this exact task and its source revision. State the start, work done, evidence, result, gaps, and next owner. Keep failed, partial, and blocked work visible. Writing the record does not authorize publishing it.

Use one stable execution ID for this task’s actual run. Internal retries, checks, and new versions do not add runs. A separately scoped child task may have its own ID linked to the parent. A teaching example has no real execution ID and must not enter the run count. Follow the [recipe and meta-article guide](https://localservicespotlight.com/meta-articles/) for that distinction.

# Access Content Factory source assets

You need the right files before you can start a job. This guide helps you find the photos and clips your team needs. Start with the job name and file list, then check that each file will open.

**The path:** Known task and files → Approved access → Open real sources → Handoff.

**Use this when:** An assigned content task needs specific photos, videos, or project files that are not yet accessible.

## Inputs
- The assigned project and task, your work email, the files or dates you need, and the intended use.
- The project’s current access contact and approved invitation or credential-sharing method. The public guide names an operations contact and LastPass; confirm that this is still the approved route for this project.
- The exact Basecamp project and known asset locations. The source names Google Photos, Drive, and Dropbox, but this task grants no access to unrelated libraries.
- A way to record safe file references, access results, and blockers without copying passwords, recovery codes, or private customer content.

## First-run prompt

> Use my assigned project, file list, and approved access method to build an access checklist. Prepare a narrow request if needed, but do not send without authority. Check each actual file and separate viewing, downloading, editing, and publication rights. Report exact blockers without storing or exposing secrets.

## Steps
1. Write the access scope before asking: project, task, work email, specific source files, intended use, and the role you need. Ask the project’s known access owner to confirm the current method. Do not use a public article’s historical shared-login email as a credential instruction.
2. Prepare the request for the approved operations contact. Send it only within the authority of the actual job. A draft request is not an invitation, and an invitation is not working access.
3. Accept the genuine project invitation. If the access owner confirms LastPass is still used, accept that invitation into the approved account and use the shared item for this project. If the project uses direct account access instead, follow that invitation. Do not create a second credential store or put secrets in the tracker.
4. Open the assigned Basecamp project through the confirmed link. Check the task, source-file instructions, and allowed uses. Use [Basecamp Basics](https://localservicespotlight.com/basecamp-basics-the-foundation-of-how-we-work/) for the team’s project workflow; it is a reference, not a grant of access.
5. Open the confirmed source location. In Photos, search by the supplied person, date, place, or event; in Drive or Dropbox, follow the exact project folder. A search result with a similar name is only a candidate: compare the source date, subject, and task.
6. Check the actual required files one by one. Confirm the photo or video is the intended source, the original or allowed copy is available, and your role permits the needed next action. Keep video muted at volume zero; use metadata, still frames, or captions if silence cannot be verified before playback.
7. Log file reference, system, expected action, observed access, date, and any use limits. Distinguish “can view” from “can download,” “can edit,” or “may publish.” These are separate checks, not one yes/no permission.
8. For missing access, record the exact denied location or missing file and send the smallest request through the current authorized project route. Do not widen sharing, seek another person’s login, or infer that every asset is cleared.
9. Hand the verified source list to [Upload the source to Drive and Descript](https://local-service-spotlight.github.io/task-library/?task=step-1-upload-video-to-google-drive-and-descript#task-step-1-upload-video-to-google-drive-and-descript) or the specific assigned processing task. Report completion in the project thread only when sending is authorized. Keep inaccessible files as blockers, and write the run record even when access is incomplete.

## Definition of done (QA checklist)

- [ ] The project, task, files, intended use, and requested role are explicit.
- [ ] The assigned project opens and the actual required source files have been checked.
- [ ] View, download, edit, and publication rights are distinguished according to the task.
- [ ] Missing files or access are recorded precisely; no historical login detail is treated as current proof.
- [ ] The handoff contains safe file references and limits, with no secrets.

## Example(s)

**Fictional teaching example — no access was requested or granted.** A sample assignment asks an editor to use two Maple Cycle photos and one recorded shop tour.

| Needed item | Sample observed state | Next action |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Shop front photo | Can open the intended file; use approved for the draft | Pass its private file reference to the editor |
| Owner photo | Search finds two people with the same first name | Ask the project owner to confirm identity |
| Shop tour | Folder opens, but the video cannot be downloaded | Ask for the role needed for the stated editing task |

The sample result is one verified source, one identity question, and one access blocker. “The folder opens” would hide two unfinished checks. No password, shared-login address, or private file URL belongs in a public meta article.

## Handoff and Content Factory context

The assigned editor gets the verified source references and use limits. [Upload the source to Drive and Descript](https://local-service-spotlight.github.io/task-library/?task=step-1-upload-video-to-google-drive-and-descript#task-step-1-upload-video-to-google-drive-and-descript) is the common next task; use another processing task only when the assignment names it. The agent can prepare the plan, organize allowed files, and check the evidence it can actually access. A person records real stories, supplies permission, or resolves an account step when needed. For all agent media checks, keep the player muted and its volume at zero before playback. If that cannot be checked, use captions, metadata, or still frames. Do not claim sound quality was heard when it was not.

# Create Dollar a Day ad creatives

An ad works best with a clear point worth sharing. This guide helps you turn a post with real response into files for a small test. Start with the source post and its measured results.

**The path:** Measured source → Placement brief → Useful variants → Checked creative handoff.

**Use this when:** The promotion owner requests creative files from content with documented organic signal.

## Inputs
- The real post/clip/article and its observed metrics, measurement date and comparison period.
- The [Goals, Content, and Targeting](https://blitzmetrics.com/gct-business-strategy/) brief and intended campaign/placement, audience and content rights.
- Current specifications for those exact placements and access to an existing design/video editor.
- The Content Library folder, requested variant count and named promotion owner. Creative preparation does not itself spend money.

## First-run prompt

> Prepare the requested ad files from this source and dated organic evidence. Keep the claim true, inspect current placement specs, and make clearly tracked variants. Return checked assets and a test hypothesis. Keep untested ideas labeled and do not spend or launch outside the separate campaign scope.

## Steps
1. Read the organic evidence and why this content was chosen under [Dollar a Day](https://blitzmetrics.com/dad/). A view, share or comment is a signal, not proof of sales. If no evidence exists, prepare a clearly untested concept only if requested, and route validation to Post rather than marking it a winner.
2. Write a brief for each actual placement: purpose, asset type, ratio, duration, text fields, landing page and rights. Check current provider requirements; Facebook feed, Stories and YouTube formats do not share one universal size.
3. Keep the source’s supported claim and context. Adapt it for sound-off understanding with readable text/captions. Do not add a new performance promise just because the asset is now an ad.
4. Create the agreed variants, commonly two or three under the source method. Change one meaningful feature such as the opening crop or headline, and record the difference. Variant results are unknown until tested.
5. Export for the selected placements and inspect visible safe areas so controls will not cover the speaker, caption or key point. Google supports different ratios by format; YouTube does not mean horizontal-only.
6. Check copy lengths in the actual placement preview and verify the canonical landing URL. A provider preview passing does not certify the truth of a claim or approval of an ad.
7. Name each file by date/source/platform/variant and store it in the actual creative folder, using 04-Promote-Creatives when that is the project convention. Record dimensions, duration, file path, source-post ID and metric receipt.
8. Hand over the package with the hypothesis, difference between variants and unresolved eligibility checks. Launching, targeting and spend follow the separate already-authorized campaign task, not an automatic action caused by exporting files.

## Definition of done (QA checklist)

- [ ] Each selected winner has actual dated organic evidence, or is explicitly an untested requested concept.
- [ ] Claims, rights, caption text and source context are preserved.
- [ ] Each requested placement has a checked final export and clearly named variant.
- [ ] The handoff records the test hypothesis and real readiness; no campaign or revenue result is invented.

## Example(s)

**Fictional teaching example — no ad or real metrics.** A sample shop post got six useful customer questions over seven days. That invented teaching signal suggests testing its photo checklist; it does not prove sales.

Variant A opens with “Show the whole bike.” Variant B opens with “Help the shop see the issue.” Both use the same source demonstration and preserve the need for an inspection. The delivery sheet records which crop and line changed, the requested placement, and “test not launched.” It does not add a $1/day schedule or claim either version won.

## Handoff and Content Factory context

The promotion owner receives the assets for [Run the scoped Dollar a Day campaign](https://local-service-spotlight.github.io/task-library/?task=run-dollar-a-day-campaign-on-winning-content#task-run-dollar-a-day-campaign-on-winning-content) when its own inputs and authority are ready.

Produce supplies the real source. **Process**, this stage of the [Content Factory](https://blitzmetrics.com/content-factory/), turns it into useful finished assets. Post saves or publishes them on the agreed channels. Promote tests and distributes suitable work within its own scope. The handoff above names this task’s actual next step; catalog neighbors alone are not prerequisites.

## When this runs

Per selected source and defined creative batch. New variants follow observed test evidence; this task creates no recurring ad spend.

## First-run setup and continuity

Open the supplied task file and its linked source. Verify the project’s real inputs, account, access and output folder before work. This Markdown file is a guide; it does not install an app, connect an account, supply a subscription or create a schedule. Carry out work already authorized; do not ask for the same approval again. Keep any unsupplied destination or new action outside that scope clearly pending.

Save source IDs, versions, decisions, checked outputs and next owner in the project tracker. Before a retry, check the saved state and other workers’ changes. A model name does not guarantee memory or a running timer. Repeated work needs an actual configured trigger and durable state; one-off work can be started by the prompt above.

Keep agent media muted with volume zero before playback. If mute cannot be verified, use captions, metadata or still frames. State the limit: silent visual checks do not prove spoken-word accuracy or audio quality. Do not start sound through the user’s speakers unless explicitly asked.

## Write up the real run

For every actual attempt, [write its meta article](https://blitzmetrics.com/meta-article-prompt/) with this recipe and revision, trigger, steps performed, output evidence, measured result, gaps and next owner. Failed, blocked and partial attempts also get a written record. A draft can satisfy writing; publishing it follows the existing job scope.

Keep one stable execution ID across retries and edits. A separately scoped child task may have its own ID linked to its parent. Writing the parent’s meta record is part of that run, not an endless new chain. The [recipe and meta-article guide](https://localservicespotlight.com/meta-articles/) explains this distinction. Teaching examples are not real executions and must not enter the run count.

# Create quote cards from strongest statements

A short quote can help a reader remember a good point. This guide turns a real statement into a clear card. Start with the checked words and the person who said them.

**The path:** Checked quote → Real attribution → Readable card → Source-linked export.

**Use this when:** A source has concise, context-safe statements worth turning into attributed graphic assets.

## Inputs
- The verified transcript and original source times, with rights to quote and reuse the material.
- The speaker’s verified full name and relevant company/role, plus a permitted real photo when available.
- The brand’s design rules, actual destination sizes and existing design tool.
- The source/asset tracker and requested number of cards.

## First-run prompt

> Find source-safe exact quotes and prepare the requested cards. Check surrounding context, attribution and image rights. Keep direct quotes verbatim, label summaries, inspect the final export at phone size, and save source timestamps. Do not invent a speaker, image, endorsement or publication.

## Steps
1. Find one- or two-sentence statements that make sense without hidden context. Check the surrounding source for a condition or limitation that must remain.
2. Copy the quote exactly from the checked source and record its time. If it needs paraphrasing, label it a summary and design it without quotation marks; do not quietly rewrite a direct quote.
3. Select the strongest usable set within the request. Three to five is a source planning suggestion, not a reason to invent weak or unsupported quotes.
4. Confirm attribution and permissions. A first name, domain-only praise or unknown speaker is not a publishable testimonial. If the photo is missing, record that need or prepare a clearly identified text layout instead of using a stock face.
5. Set the quote in large, high-contrast type with the real attribution nearby. Use the speaker’s permitted image where supplied and keep the design tied to the statement rather than implying an endorsement beyond it.
6. Size the card for the actual destination and inspect it at phone/thumbnail scale. Keep text clear of crops and platform overlays. Add accessible post text describing the quote rather than relying only on pixels.
7. Compare the final exported words with the transcript, including negatives, numbers and punctuation that changes meaning. Verify that the photo and attribution belong to this speaker.

# Extract 15–60 second clips from long-form video

A long video may hold a short answer worth sharing. This guide helps you cut one clear point that can stand on its own. Start with the source and the place where the clip will be used.

**The path:** Source moment → Complete short idea → Captioned export → Checked clip list.

**Use this when:** A timestamped source has useful standalone moments for a defined short-clip deliverable.

## Inputs
- The source recording, verified timestamped transcript, GCT and rights to edit/reuse it.
- The exact source version or cleaned cut, with a mapping to original time if editing changed its clock.
- A working editor such as Descript, actual export access, and current requirements for the planned destination.
- The clip tracker, intended count if agreed, named editor and posting/promotion owner.

## First-run prompt

> Find and prepare standalone 15–60-second clips for the specified channels from this real source. Check surrounding context, preserve source times, add accurate captions and verify actual exports. Record the real number made and pending audio checks. Do not invent highlights, guarantee reach, publish or launch ads outside the job’s scope.

## Steps
1. Read the full timestamped source and list candidate ideas with start/end times. Choose a point that helps the intended reader; do not promise ten or twenty clips from an hour regardless of its content.
2. Check context before and after each candidate. Preserve conditions, speaker identity and meaning. A dramatic sentence that reverses the full discussion is not a good standalone clip.
3. For this task, target 15–60 seconds as the house brief, not a universal platform limit. If a complete useful idea cannot fit, choose another moment or explicitly propose a longer asset instead of cutting away the necessary qualification.
4. Create a separate composition for each selected clip. Trim near natural phrase boundaries and check the opening quickly states a useful point. The first few seconds matter editorially, but no three-second hook test guarantees views.
5. Use any filler cleanup selectively. It is optional, not a prerequisite that must consume AI credits before every cut. Preserve the source version and avoid synthetic speech that misrepresents what was recorded.
6. Frame for the actual destination: choose an agreed portrait, square or landscape layout, and keep the speaker, key action and readable captions inside it. Verify current destination requirements rather than assuming all feeds use the same dimensions.
7. Add accurate visible captions or the requested subtitle track. Descript SRT/VTT export is a separate artifact; it does not by itself burn captions into the video. Check names, line breaks and the final exported frame.
8. Export a local finished file or the specifically authorized share destination. Confirm duration, dimensions, complete idea, caption readability and file integrity. A plan-dependent export setting cannot create detail missing from the original.
9. Save one row per actual clip with source ID/times, cut version, hook, duration, dimensions, output path and next use. Record actual count and any audio review still pending. Route suitable clips to posts or ad-creative preparation; exporting a clip does not publish it or authorize spend.

## Definition of done (QA checklist)

- [ ] Each clip is a complete source-faithful idea in the agreed 15–60-second brief or has an explicit exception.
- [ ] Source/cut timestamps and rights are recorded.
- [ ] Final exports have checked dimensions, duration and accurate readable captions.
- [ ] Actual exported count, audio review state and next owner are logged without performance or publication claims.

The clip title is “Say when the noise starts.” Its row records original source 03:10–03:42, the separate cut version, portrait layout if the planned channel calls for it, and “caption/export checks pending” until the file exists. # Grade article using Jennifer

A polished article can still have a wrong fact or weak proof. This guide helps you check it with a named set of rules. Start with the full draft, its source, and the rules you will use.

**The path:** Exact draft and rubric → Evidence-based findings → Bounded fixes → Clear readiness decision.

**Use this when:** A finished draft needs a bounded, recorded quality review before its next publishing step.

## Inputs
- The complete versioned article, GCT, page role, transcript/primary proof, visuals, links and author context.
- The actual Jennifer rubric file/version and current [Article Guidelines](https://localservicespotlight.com/article-guidelines/) plus task standard. Jennifer is the named review rubric, not proof of a running installed agent.
- The requested review tier and revision budget, a writer for corrections, and a tracker for findings.
- Rendered page evidence when available; draft-only checks stay separate from public checks.

## First-run prompt

> Review this exact article and source using the supplied Jennifer version plus current owned standards. First list rubric conflicts. Return quoted, located findings and hard-gate states; give a letter only when the rubric supports it. Keep fixes bounded, do not manufacture proof to meet quotas, and do not equate A- with publication authority.

## Steps
1. Record the exact draft and rubric versions. Check the rubric against current standards before grading. Check for version conflicts such as unconditional A- readiness, arbitrary ten-reference/three-link quotas or claims that every personal article proves a personal relationship. Newer revisions may have already fixed some clauses; cite the exact version you inspect. Preserve those conflicts as findings instead of inventing evidence to satisfy them.
2. Use the maintained role-specific standard for hard decisions: truthful facts/relationships, attributed permitted praise, clear GCT, meaningful lead visual, correct voice, useful links, and complete task contract where applicable. A score never overrides a failed proof, relationship, attribution, or compliance gate. Apply the named credibility caps from the canonical source: a Trophy-name paragraph without a specific shared scene, reader lesson, and primary source is capped; a Relationship noun outruns the evidence when the article claims a stronger bond than its source proves; Repeated defensive caveats or verification theater are capped unless a legal, regulatory, or compliance disclosure materially requires them; Public copy exposes internal scoring or production metadata when it publishes internal proof IDs, scores, or repurposing instructions that are not the article's topic; and praise that is anonymous or attributed only to a domain/company remains `publish_ready: false` and HOLD until it has the required named source, exact quote, and permission. Do not silently call a revised rubric the unchanged legacy Jennifer.
3. Review the full article, media/alt/caption context, source and available rendering. Quote each real defect and identify its location, violated rule, severity, evidence and requested fix. A count of names or links is not proof of quality.
4. Return structured review fields: draft revision, rubric revision, rubric conflicts, grade if a consistent rubric supports one, publish_ready, hard-gate states and actionable findings. Use grade UNKNOWN when unresolved rubric conflicts prevent a defensible letter; do not mint a flattering substitute score.
5. Keep publish_ready false while a hard gate fails or required evidence is untested. Under a reconciled Jennifer rubric, A- or A can end cosmetic iteration only after applicable hard checks pass. A letter never grants publication authority.
6. Send exact defects to the writer. Preserve the source budget when used: STRONG up to three rounds, MODERATE two, LIGHT one; tier targets do not waive hard gates. At the budget limit, return the remaining list and next decision rather than looping indefinitely.
7. Recheck the changed revision and affected sources. Do not regrade unchanged accepted copy to chase an A, but a substantive new change or newly failed hard gate requires a new check of the current revision.

# How to inventory a podcast on YouTube

Good interviews can get lost in a busy channel. This guide helps you list them, check who is in each one, and choose what to use next. Start with the exact channel and a shared sheet.

**The path:** Channel and playlists → Unique episodes → Verified people → Ranked source queue.

**Use this when:** A channel’s podcast-format videos need an evidence-backed inventory for reuse.

## Inputs
- The exact channel ID/URL, host names/variants, series names and existing inventory.
- A client-owned sheet with Playlists, All Episodes, Cross-Platform, Guests and Summary tabs; use the linked guide’s template when available.
- Read access to YouTube and primary episode/show pages, and authorized API quota if using the Data API.
- The intended scope/date range, access limits, metric observation time and next content owner.

## First-run prompt

> Inventory this exact YouTube channel into the five-tab format. Reconcile playlists, videos, live items and searches by video ID; verify guests and public dates. Keep inaccessible rows and metric gaps visible. Calculate transparent summaries and a source-backed priority list without claiming every appearance worldwide was found.

## Steps
1. Create or update one dedicated inventory. Record channel ID, scope, date and search coverage. Keep source rows and summary formulas separate.
2. Map playlists with title, URL, observed count and type. Treat long duration, guest names and “podcast” as discovery clues; inspect the content before classifying it as an interview.
3. Capture each accessible episode with unique video ID, title, series, duration, public date, observed views, guest/host role and source URL. Follow all playlist pages/API nextPageToken values. Keep playlist memberships separately so one video in two playlists remains one episode.
4. Search beyond playlists through Videos, Live and relevant channel queries. The source suggests at least ten targeted searches when useful; record terms and outcomes rather than calling ten queries proof of completeness. Include known names and series variants.
5. Verify each guest from a primary title/description/show page or checked introduction. Use “Solo — host” only when supported. Keep unknown people and inaccessible/private/deleted slots as explicit exceptions rather than invented rows.
6. Build one Guests row per verified person with relevant identity links and episode list. A missing LinkedIn URL is a documented exception, not permission to guess a profile.
7. Cross-check Listen Notes, Podchaser, the host’s site and global YouTube results. Store outside-channel appearances in Cross-Platform and preserve source links. Discovery results and AI suggestions remain leads until verified.
8. For comparable videos with known dates and views, calculate lifetime average views per day using the stated observation time and age rule. It is not recent velocity. Keep same-day/unknown-date rows unranked or explicitly use a disclosed one-day denominator; do not silently divide by zero.
9. Build Summary totals from unique accessible verified rows, plus separate unresolved/unavailable counts. Rank within comparable groups. If using top 20%, state the eligible denominator and rounding rule; retrieve permitted transcripts for selected rows, retain timestamped originals and record actual word counts.
10. Reconcile playlist memberships, unique episodes, exceptions, guest identity and summary formulas. Log a quoted-title search as a dated query/result observation, not guaranteed Google indexing. Hand over priority sources, coverage limits and measured time/cost only when recorded.

## Definition of done (QA checklist)

- [ ] All five tabs exist with exact channel/scope and a reproducible coverage log.
- [ ] Unique video IDs are deduplicated while playlist membership and unavailable slots remain visible.
- [ ] People, dates, metrics and transcripts are verified or labeled unknown with reasons.
- [ ] Summary totals, priority denominator and formula choices reconcile to source rows.

## Example(s)

**Fictional teaching example — no channel was audited.** Playlist A lists five videos; Playlist B lists four, with two IDs shared. The inventory has seven unique listed videos, not nine. One is unavailable, leaving six accessible rows and one exception.

For a sample video with 600 observed views over 30 days, lifetime average is 20 views/day. That does not prove it got 20 views yesterday. If five rows have comparable valid metrics, the top 20% selection is one row. The summary shows the date and denominator rather than calling that row a sales winner.
